The farthingale is a hooped or structured petticoat that creates a distinctive bell-shaped or cone-shaped silhouette in women's skirts, worn predominantly in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Originating in Spain and spreading across Europe, the farthingale became essential to Elizabethan and Renaissance fashion, transforming women's bodies into architectural monuments of fabric and frame.

Constructed from linen with horizontal hoops of wood, bone, or whale baleen that flare outward from the waist, the Spanish farthingale created a cone, while the English version produced a bell shape. The Spanish farthingale could extend as wide as forty-eight inches at the hem, making doorways a genuine hazard and requiring women to turn sideways to pass through. The garment required multiple layers of skirts and petticoats over the hoop structure; the weight and bulk made movement difficult and sitting nearly impossible in narrow chairs.

Farthingales rose and fell in width according to fashion cycles. The most extreme versions required wearers to sit on cushions rather than chairs. The garment became intertwined with Elizabethan court culture under Queen Elizabeth I, who wore progressively more extravagant versions as a display of royal authority and fashion leadership. The farthingale was associated with moral controversy; some religious authorities condemned it as a device of vanity and deception, distorting the natural female form.

The farthingale was gradually superseded by the crinoline in the nineteenth century, which offered similar silhouette with simpler construction. The garment works in close relation with the corset, the rigid undergarment worn simultaneously to shape the torso while the farthingale shaped the skirt. Its prominence in formal dress links it to the ruff, the elaborate neckwear that paired with farthingales as part of high Renaissance formal dress. The farthingale became synonymous with Elizabeth I, the English queen who made the extravagant farthingale a symbol of Elizabethan court power and fashion innovation. The technology endured into the nineteenth century through the crinoline, the later hooped petticoat that achieved similar silhouettes with hooped petticoats.
